● Yes, I think this fits ARGUS better than the current SaaS layout. Here's why,
  what I'd change, and which libraries I'd use.

  Why it fits

  Your hackathon rule is "the replay is the product, make the AI visible." Right
  now the dashboard is a left nav with pages and cards, so the video, the
  sources, the models and the products are on separate pages. An OBS-style
  studio puts them all on one screen, so you can watch the stream, see which
  Meta model is working on it, and see the data products fill in, all at once.
  That's what you want judges to see.

  How OBS maps to ARGUS

  ┌──────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │     OBS      │                          ARGUS                           │
  ├──────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Scene        │ Project (one project = one studio, like you said)        │
  │ collection   │                                                          │
  ├──────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Scenes       │ Data products: switching one changes what the preview    │
  │              │ shows and which panels open                              │
  ├──────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Sources dock │ Sources (video, CSV, API…), with live/paused status and  │
  │              │ an add button                                            │
  ├──────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Preview /    │ Stream: video with the model's boxes and masks drawn on  │
  │ Program      │ top                                                      │
  ├──────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │              │ Model mixer: one meter per Meta model (vision,           │
  │ Audio mixer  │ segmentation, reasoning, verify) showing calls, latency  │
  │              │ and confidence                                           │
  ├──────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Controls     │ Run / Pause / Record replay / Share                      │
  ├──────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Status bar   │ Rows · jobs · model calls · last frame time              │
  ├──────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Docks        │ Small data-product panels (your widgets) that can be     │
  │              │ resized, tabbed and rearranged                           │
  └──────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌ ARGUS ▸ Bridge Intelligence ▾ ─────────────────────── ● LIVE  ⏺ Record  
  Share ┐
  │ ┌────────────────── STREAM ─────────────────┐ ┌─ Count ──┐ ┌─ Share ──┐     
   │
  │ │  video + model boxes/masks                │ │ 1,284 ▲  │ │  ◔ ring  │     
   │
  │ │                                           │ ├─ Heat ───┤ ├─ Feed ───┤     
   │
  │ └──── ◀ ▮▮ ▶ ──────●──────────── 02:14 ─────┘ │ ▦▦▦▦     │ │ 14:02 …  │     
   │
  ├─ Products ─┬─ Sources ─────┬─ Model mixer ────────────────┬─ Controls 
  ────────┤
  │ ▸ Traffic  │ ● bridge-cam  │ Vision    ▇▇▇▇▇▁ 42 calls    │ ▶ Run   ⏸ Pause 
   │
  │   People   │ ○ weather.csv │ Segment   ▇▇▇▁▁▁ 18          │ ⏺ Record replay 
   │
  │   + Add    │ + Add source  │ Reason    ▇▁▁▁▁▁  3          │                 
   │
  └────────────┴───────────────┴──────────────────────────────┴─────────────────
  ──┘
   rows 12,401 · jobs 2 running · model calls 63 · last frame 0.4s ago

  The same layout, read-only, can also become the /explore replay viewer, so
  visitors get the studio view of the run you recorded. That one change probably
  shows off the most for the hackathon.

  Libraries

  - The layout: shadcn Resizable. It's built on react-resizable-panels, matches
    your shadcn base-nova setup, and adds one command: bunx shadcn add 
    resizable. It covers the fixed OBS layout with resizable panels. Start here.
  - Drag-and-drop docks: dockview. Add it only if you want users to drag panels
    around, tab them together or pop them out the way OBS docks work. It's the
    best React docking library right now: no dependencies, with tabs, floating
    panels and pop-out windows. I'd add it in phase 2 for the widget area only.
  - Video: plain <video> plus a <canvas>/SVG overlay for the model boxes. You
    don't need a video SDK, because you're replaying stored frames, not
    streaming live.
  - Keep: your existing widgets in src/widgets/library/, which become the small
    dock panels, plus lucide, motion and recharts.

  Caveats

  - Sources without video: for projects whose sources are CSV or API only, the
    Stream panel needs a fallback, like a live table or the flow graph.
  - Mobile: OBS layouts are desktop-only, so on phones I'd stack the panels.
  - Pages: Agents, Flows and Assistant would turn into docks or tabs inside the
    studio instead of separate pages. That's a real change to how people move
    around the app.

  Plan (following the AGENTS.md component-first rule)

  1. Build src/components/studio/ with the studio shell, stream preview, sources
     dock, model mixer, controls, status bar and widget docks.
  2. Add them to /design as STU-01…STU-07, each with its empty, loading, live
     and replay states, using your replay sample data.
  3. After they look right in /design, replace the (app) layout and /dashboard
     with the studio, and point /explore at the read-only version.

  Should I start on steps 1–2, building the studio components and putting them
  in /design so you can see the result before any routes change?

● The OBS-style studio is built and previewed in /design. Following the
  component-first rule in AGENTS.md, I haven't wired it into /dashboard yet.

  Open it: http://localhost:3000/design/studio fills the whole browser window,
  and the F key goes true full screen. All the variants are on /design#studio.

  What's on screen

  - Program view (center): a live canvas bridge cam with each model's output
    drawn on it. SAM 3.1 adds colored person masks, boxes and track IDs with
    confidence, and Muse Spark adds a caption that types out at the bottom. A
    green flash marks each frame sent to the models. A person only gets a box
    once their frame has actually been processed, so the model's delay is
    visible.
  - Right side: the selected data product at full size, with a strip of small
    live tiles for the others. Click a tile to switch, like scenes in OBS.
  - Bottom docks:
    - Data products: the scene list.
    - Sources: each video source lists the layers each model draws, with an eye
      toggle per layer.
    - Model mixer: one strip per model, with a level meter (green/amber/red,
      peak hold), call count, average latency, its last output and a pause
      button. Pausing SAM removes its masks from the stream.
    - Model log: every call. Amber lines mark frames where the code's count
      overruled Muse's.
    - Controls: Start/Stop, Record replay, Share.
  - Status bar: in replay mode it reads "0 new model calls · $0.00", which makes
    the hackathon point.
  - Layout: every divider can be dragged. Space plays or pauses, the arrow keys
    step one frame, and 1–5 switch products. On phones the docks stack.

  Library: I used shadcn Resizable, which is built on react-resizable-panels v4.
  Your existing widgets render inside the docks unchanged.

  What it was tested on

  - Typecheck, lint and all 132 tests pass.
  - I took screenshots at 1920×1080, inside /design, and at phone width, with no
    console errors.

  The demo is still a simulated run: the bridge video is drawn on a canvas, and
  the counts and model calls are generated in src/components/studio/sim.ts. SAM
  3.1 shows up as if it were working, but your 0.3.0 doc says it still has to be
  confirmed on your API key.

  Files:
  - New: src/components/studio/ (studio shell, docks, stream canvas, sim,
    /design kit), src/app/design/studio/page.tsx,
    src/components/ui/resizable.tsx.
  - Edited: src/app/design/page.tsx, which gets the STU-01…06 surfaces.
  - package.json and bun.lock got the new dependency.

  Other changes appeared in the repo while I worked (landing page, globals.css,
  marketing layout). I didn't touch those. Nothing is committed.

  Next steps (once you like the look)

  1. Make /dashboard render the studio for the current project, fed by real
     Observations, sources and job state instead of sim.ts.
  2. Have the /explore replays use the same studio in replay mode, reading
     recorded runs.
  3. Show a real video plus stored SAM and Muse responses in place of the drawn
     canvas, once a recorded run exists.

  Should I start on step 1?

● The old dashboard is gone, and every project now has its own studio at
  /studio/[id]. Setup opens as dialog windows over the Studio, so you never
  leave it. Typecheck and lint are clean and the tests pass (132 pass, 0 fail).
  I haven't opened a signed-in /studio/[id] with a real project, because that
  needs an account in your database.

  Routes
  - /studio/[id] is a project's studio. If the project isn't yours you're sent
    to /projects, and if you're signed out you're sent to /login.
  - /studio opens the project you had open last, or /projects if there isn't
    one.
  - Old /dashboard/... links redirect to /studio.
  - Opening or creating a project lands on /studio/<its id>. The project
    chooser's button now says "Open in Studio →".
  - Visiting /studio/[id] makes that project the open one, so all the existing
    actions (uploads, adding sources and so on) apply to the project in the URL.
    This is set in src/proxy.ts.

  Setup windows
  - src/components/studio/studio-window.tsx holds the list of windows. To add a
    setup screen, add an entry there and pass its content to <Studio 
    windows={...}>.
  - The first window is Sources, which is the old sources page moved into the
    window: add source, timelines and lanes, video upload, camera capture,
    weather and sensor setup, and webhooks. You open it from the menu bar, from
    the + and gear buttons in the Sources dock, or from "Add a source" in an
    empty project.
  - It's previewed in /design as STU-07. I screenshotted it open over the
    running stream, with no console errors.

  Removed (66 files)
  - The whole (app) route group: overview, products, agents, flows, assistant,
    alerts, admin, bridge, connect, observations, replay and sources.
  - The sidebar, the flow editor UI, chat-actions.ts, and 13 components only the
    dashboard used.

    components/workspace/. The project chooser, the new-project pages and the
    explore replay use them.

● The new /projects page is ready to demo, and the migration is applied to your
  database.

  What /projects is now: you said it should be a place to look at your data
  products, like a small dashboard, with the complicated work happening in ARGUS
  Studio. That's how it's built:
  - One project per slide, filling the whole screen. The left panel shows the
    project's number and type, its name, a description, counts of products,
    sources and rows, the data sources with their live status, and a big Open in
    ARGUS Studio button. Edit, Share and Delete sit under it.
  - The products are drawn as large as the screen allows. One product fills the
    stage, two sit side by side, four make a 2×2 grid, and five or six make
    three across. The charts stretch to fill their tiles, so there's no empty
    space under them. Clicking a product opens the Studio to configure it.
  - A filmstrip along the bottom shows every project as a thumbnail, plus a "New
    project" tile.
  - For the demo: Present (or the F key) goes browser full screen, ← → move
    between projects, and Enter opens the Studio.
  - Descriptions are new. The new-project dialog now asks "What it watches" as
    an optional field. For projects you already have, use Edit on the slide to
    add a name and description.

  Checks: the type check, lint and all 132 tests pass. I took screenshots of the
  full-size preview at 1920×1080, stepped through it with the arrow keys, and
  saw no console errors. I couldn't check the real /projects page with your
  account, because that needs you signed in.

  Things to know:
  - /projects no longer uses the hub layout with its narrow column. It's full
    screen now, and your email and sign-out button moved into the deck's top
    bar.
  - The old slide carousel is deleted. In /design, the deck replaced PRJ-01 and
    PRJ-02, and you can see it at full size at /design/projects.
  - Three chart widgets (stat-trend, volume-bars, heat-grid) now stretch when
    their container has a set height. On other pages they look the same as
    before.
  - The migration also added the track field on folders, which the folder
    tracker needs. I haven't built that feature yet. Turning mood, workout and
    food files into tracked values in Sources folders is what I'll do next.

  Nothing is committed.

> hey do u think that the ai assitant you remove form the old dashboard should  
  eb apart of the projects page per page chat ??                                

● Yes, I think it belongs there, with a few limits.

  Why it fits: /projects is where people look at their data products, and "what
  does this mean?" is the first thing they'll ask while looking. A chat per
  project ("Ask about Harbor Bridge") answers right on the slide. It also helps
  the demo: judges see the Meta model reading your data on screen, not hidden
  behind it.

  How I'd shape it:
  - One chat per project. It's tied to the slide you're on, so it only sees that
    project's products and sources. Moving to another slide switches the chat.
  - A drawer you open, not a fixed panel. An "Ask" button on the slide opens it
    from the right, and the products shrink to make room. Closed, the slide
    stays clean for presenting.
  - For questions only. The chat reads the project's Observations and product
    rows, then answers and points to the product or rows it used. If you ask it
    to change something, it sends you to the Studio. That keeps your split: look
    in /projects, configure in the Studio.
  - Honest numbers. This follows the roadmap rule that models propose and code
    computes. The model picks what to query, deterministic code calculates the
    counts and averages, and the model explains them. It doesn't invent numbers.
  - Starter questions on each project. For example "What was busiest today?" or
    "Anything unusual?", so a judge can click one instead of typing.

  One catch: /explore is meant to run with no model calls. So on public replays
  the chat would show recorded questions and answers, not live ones.

  Getting the old code back: the deletion isn't committed, so the old assistant
  (chat-actions.ts, the assistant pages and chat-list) is still in git. I'd
  reuse its model and message-saving code and build new UI as a drawer component
  in /design first.

  Should I build it like this? The folder tracker is still waiting too, so tell
  me which one to do first.

● I think both are worth doing. Much of the groundwork is already in the code.

  1. AI chat: a small "Ask" button in the top bar

  I'd put it in the /projects header, beside Present. Clicking it opens a narrow
  panel from the right, and it answers about whichever project slide you're on.

  - It only answers questions. You set things up in the Studio, and the chat
    helps you understand them. For example: "What was the busiest hour?" or "Why
    did this alert fire?"
  - The model picks the query, code does the maths. Every number in an answer
    comes from your real data, and the reply shows which product or source it
    came from. That keeps your rule that models propose and code computes, and
    it looks good in front of judges.
  - Starter questions under the input, so a judge doesn't face an empty box.
  - The old chat backend still exists. src/app/api/chat/route.ts can already
    look up files, products, Observations and alerts. Mostly I'd be building the
    new panel and narrowing it to one project.
  - On /explore it would show saved questions and answers. Visitors don't
    trigger model calls.

  2. Alerts: "if this passes X, tell me"

  There are already two pieces:
  - An alerts table, with evidence linking each alert to the Observations that
    triggered it.
  - An agent flow that drafts alerts and waits for a human to approve them.

  What's missing is user-set thresholds. My design:

  - Rule: a product's number, a condition, a value, and a time window. Examples:
    "People count > 50 for 5 min", or "Mood < 3 for 3 days in a row".
  - Code checks the rules, not the model. Each new Observation is checked
    against the rules, so an alert fires for an exact, provable reason.
  - The AI adds context after an alert fires. A Meta model writes the
    explanation ("crowding at the north gate, 3 camera frames attached"). It can
    also suggest a sensible threshold from your past data, which you accept or
    change.
  - Where you see alerts:
    - Studio: an Alerts window where you set rules (another pop-up window, as
      you asked), plus an alert log panel.
    - /projects: a red dot on the slide and its filmstrip thumbnail, and an
      alert list on the slide.
  - Notifications: in-app only at first. Email or push can come later.

  Order I'd suggest

  1. A Products window in the Studio. The empty projects now say "set up in
     studio", so this has to exist. Alert rules also belong to a product.
  2. Alerts. Code checks the rules; the AI explains each alert.
  3. The Ask chat. It's more useful once there are alerts to ask about.
  4. The folder tracker. Mood, workout and food data also feed alerts nicely
     ("alert me if I skip workouts 3 days").

  Should I start with the Products window and then alerts? Or would you rather
  have the chat first, since it's the most visible AI piece for the demo?

● Yes, I think a universal chat with @-mentions is better than one chat per
  project.

  How it would work

  - One "Ask ARGUS" button in the top bar of /projects, and the same button in
    the Studio menu bar. It opens the same chat panel on either page.
  - Without an @, it answers across all your projects. For example: "Which
    project had the most alerts this week?" or "What am I tracking?"
  - Typing @ brings up a list of your projects and pins the question to the ones
    you pick. For example: "@Harbor Bridge busiest hour yesterday?" or "Compare
    @Body log and @Workout log." Mentions appear as small chips in the message.
  - It starts on the project you're viewing. On a project's slide, or inside its
    Studio, the chat starts with that project already mentioned, and you can
    remove it.
  - @ could reach further later: @People count for one data product, or @alerts.
    Projects come first.

  Why I like it

  - It matches your split. /projects is where you consume your data, and one
    assistant over all of it fits that.
  - Comparing projects only works with a universal chat. "How does my sleep
    relate to my workouts?" is the kind of question that impresses judges, and a
    per-project chat can't answer it.
  - It's one chat history instead of a separate one for each project.

  Guardrails I'd keep

  - The AI only sees projects you own. An @ narrows what it looks up; it never
    widens it.
  - The model picks the query, code computes the number. Every answer shows
    where it came from, for example "from Harbor Bridge › People count, 1,240
    rows".
  - Questions only. The chat doesn't change settings; setup stays in the Studio.
    Later it could offer a button like "Create this alert?" that you confirm
    yourself.
  - On /explore it plays saved conversations, so visitors don't trigger model
    calls.

  What's already there

  - The old /api/chat route already has tools to look up data. It currently
    works on one project, and I'd change it to take the list of @-mentioned
    projects.
  - The chats table already exists. It needs a column to record which projects
    each message mentioned.

  Revised order

  1. A Products window in the Studio.
  2. Alerts.
  3. Universal Ask chat with @projects.
  4. The folder tracker.

  If you'd rather show the chat first in the demo, I can swap steps 2 and 3.
  Which should I start with?

● I've built the Ask ARGUS chat end to end, and it works in the browser. One
  thing I haven't tested: a real answer from Muse Spark. That needs META_API_KEY
  on the server and a signed-in account. Everything below was checked with
  sample data instead.

  Where it shows up
  - A pill button labelled ✨ Ask ARGUS in the /projects header and in the
    Studio menu bar. ⌘J / Ctrl+J also opens and closes it.
  - It opens as a rounded side panel that slides in from the right. It's softer
    and friendlier on purpose, unlike the square studio windows around it.

  @-mentions
  - Typing @ opens a project picker that shows each project's data products.
    Arrow keys move, Enter or Tab picks, and Esc closes it.
  - Each picked project appears as a chip. With no chips, it answers about all
    your projects. Backspace in an empty box removes the last chip.
  - If you open it from a project, that project is already tagged.
  - The welcome screen offers four starter questions that change with the
    projects tagged.

  How it stays honest
  - The model only chooses what to look up. Code works out the numbers (counts,
    min/max/mean, time span, busiest hour) from your real Observations.
  - Under each answer is a list of every lookup it made. Click one to see the
    raw data, so judges can see where each number came from.
  - The server only lets it see projects you own. It answers questions only;
    setup stays in the Studio.

  History: past chats are saved, and you can reopen or delete them. A chat
  started from a project is linked to that project. That link needed a schema
  change, and I've applied the migration (0014) to your database.

  Fixes from the final check
  - @-picker order: typing @bo put "Harbor" first, because "bo" is inside the
    word. Names where a word starts with what you typed now come first.
  - No projects yet: the panel now says "You have no projects yet. Create one in
    ARGUS Studio…" and doesn't show starter questions.

  The /design page has a new AI-01 section showing six versions of the panel:
  opened from a project, all projects, @-picker open, a recorded answer, AI not
  connected, and no projects. Type-check and lint pass, all 139 tests pass
  (including new ones for the chat logic), and the browser showed no console
  errors. Nothing is committed.

  Next I'd suggest the Products window in Studio, since the empty projects now
  say "set up in studio". After that, alerts. Later, recorded chats could be
  shown on /explore without any model calls.

● Here's my proposal for the public share page. I haven't built anything yet.

  The idea: a read-only ARGUS Studio in replay mode

  /explore/[slug] becomes the same OBS-style studio you use. It fits one screen
  with no scrolling, and it plays the project's real recorded history from the
  first day to now. Visitors can watch, scrub and click into anything, but they
  can't change anything. There's no add-source button, no settings, no recording
  and no live model calls.

  ┌ ARGUS · Harbor Bridge monitoring   PUBLIC REPLAY · shared by Aung   4 
  products · 12,480 rows   [Make your own →] ┐
  ├──────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────
  ──────────────┤
  │ SOURCES      │  [People count] [Heatmap] [Traffic] [Defects] │ HOW THE AI 
  WORKED          │
  │ ● Screen     │                                               │  Screen ──▶ 
  Muse Spark ──▶ People count
  │   ▁▃▅▇▅▃     │        PROGRAM: the chosen product,           │  Weather ─▶ 
  Llama ──────▶ Traffic
  │ ● Weather    │        as it looked at the scrubbed time      │   (lights up 
  as each job runs)
  │   ▁▁▂▂▃      │                                               
  ├────────────────────────────┤
  │ (read-only)  │                                               │ INSPECTOR 
  (click any node) │
  │              │                                               │  Muse Spark ·
  counts people│
  │              │                                               │  in: frame 
  #482 → out: {count: 7}
  │              │                                               │  model 
  proposed · code computed
  ├──────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────
  ──────────────┤
  │ ▶ 1× 4× 16×   Day 1 ─────●──────────────────────────────── now      ◆ events
                │
  │ Muse Spark ▬▬  ▬▬▬   ▬▬     Llama ▬   ▬▬    (each agent's jobs as bars on 
  the timeline)    │
  │ LOG  09:04 Muse Spark counted 7 people · 09:05 Fusion joined weather …      
                │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ───────────────┘

  What each part shows
  - Sources (left): each source with a small chart of when data arrived. This
    list is read-only.
  - Program (centre): the chosen data product, showing only rows up to the
    scrubbed time, so the chart builds up as it plays. CSV downloads stay here.
  - How the AI worked (right): the pipeline graph of sources → models/agents →
    products, which lights up as each job runs.
  - Inspector (right): click any model to see what it did. That's which model,
    its role, a sample of what went in and what came out, and labels showing
    which step the model proposed and which step code computed. This panel makes
    the AI visible to judges.
  - Timeline (bottom):
    - Play/pause, speed and drag-to-scrub, with event markers along the track.
    - One lane per agent, with a bar for each job; failed jobs are red.
    - Below it, a log that stays in sync with the play position.
  - Phones: the same parts become tabs (Program / Pipeline / Log) with the
    timeline pinned at the bottom.

  Rules

  - The numbers are real. Every number comes from recorded Observations and
    jobs. Simulated data is used only on /design.
  - No model calls on /explore. Ask ARGUS can show recorded questions and
    answers, but nobody can type a new one.
  - Privacy matches the Share dialog. Uploaded files, screen frames, keys and
    chats stay private. The Inspector shows what models produced (counts,
    labels, boxes drawn on a blank canvas), not your raw frames.

  How I'd build it

  1. Add more public-safe detail to the replay data:
     - Which model each agent used.
     - When each job started and ended.
     - One sample output Observation per agent.
     - Product rows with timestamps, so products can be filtered to the scrubbed
       time.
  2. Build the public studio as a component first, previewed on /design (EXP-01)
     with these variants: playing, mid-run, no data yet, a failed job, and
     phone.
  3. Then move /explore/[slug] onto its own full-screen layout, without the
     marketing nav or footer, and wire it to the real data.

  One decision for you: should owners be allowed to share raw screen frames as
  well? It would look more impressive, but it changes what the Share dialog
  promises. I'd keep frames private for now and show model outputs drawn on a
  blank canvas.

  Should I build it like this?

● Yes, it works. The public share page at /explore/[slug] is now a read-only
  ARGUS Studio that fits on one screen. Visitors can open photos, videos and
  screen frames, but only if you turn media sharing on for that project. It's
  off by default.

  What visitors get:
  - Top bar: project name, who shared it, and a "Public replay" badge. Visitors
    can't add sources or change anything.
  - Left: the sources, plus a Media panel of thumbnails that fills in as the
    replay plays. Clicking one opens a viewer: images show full size and videos
    play with normal controls. Each item lists what the AI found in it, has
    prev/next, and has a "Jump the replay here" button.
  - Centre: one tab per data product, showing the rows that existed at that
    moment in the replay, with CSV download. A preview of the latest media item
    sits next to it.
  - Right: the AI pipeline (which steps are a model and which are code), and an
    Inspector with two tabs. Inspect shows the model used, where it reads from,
    what it feeds, and real sample rows. Log is the event log; click an event to
    jump there.
  - Bottom: play, pause, speed and skip-quiet, plus one lane per AI step, with
    failed jobs in red.
  - Status bar: "0 new model calls · $0.00". Nothing calls a model.

  It fits 1920×1080 and phone width (390×844) with no scrolling. On phones it
  switches to three tabs.

  Share dialog: before sharing, there's an "Also show media" checkbox. Once
  shared, there's a "Show media" switch. Both say that frames can show people's
  faces. Turning the switch off deletes the frames that were kept.

  Limits you should know before demoing:
  - No old screen frames. They were deleted after analysis, as before. Frames
    are kept only from the moment media sharing is on. Uploaded photos and
    videos are available either way.
  - Findings are text only, such as "3 people" or "bench 94%". There are no
    boxes drawn on the image, because the models don't return coordinates.
  - Videos are stored and play, but the AI doesn't analyse them yet.
  - Real media hasn't been checked end to end yet. Your test project
    tSuom8XmirHq has media off, so I checked the viewer only with the samples on
    /design (EXP-02). I also haven't seen a real frame or photo load.
  - The media link returns a 500 error right now. The code is correct and works
    when run outside the server. The running next dev is still holding a schema
    from before the new "show media" column existed. Please restart next dev,
    then turn on Show media for a project and open its /explore link to check it
    with real files.

  Checks:
  - Typecheck is clean, and all 140 tests pass. I updated the frame test and
    added one that keeps a frame while media is on and deletes it when media
    goes off.
  - While writing that test I found that deleting kept frames used a storage
    call the test fake doesn't support. I changed it to the form used elsewhere
    in the same file.
  - The only lint error is in src/components/landing/explore-data.tsx, which
    isn't my file and I didn't touch.

  Nothing is committed.

> one thing about the eplay and the overall prject sis lets say this is also a

● Yes, that works, and it's the cleanest way to show what ARGUS does: one
  project, one video source, data products on top, and a replay of the whole
  run.

  The one change I'd suggest is calling the replay a view of the project, not
  another data product. A data product is the rows plus a widget, like people
  per minute. The replay is how you watch those rows being made. If replay
  became a product, every project would need it switched on, when really every
  project has it for free.

  How it fits the rules we already have:
  1. Source: the user uploads a video into the Studio's Sources window.
  2. Frames: plain code, not a model, pulls one frame every N seconds. Each
     frame records where it came from: which video and what second (e.g. 00:42).
  3. Observations: the models look at each frame and write rows, like "3 people
     at 00:42", that point back to that frame and second.
  4. Products: the manifests read those rows, the same as for photos or screen
     frames.
  5. Replay: the timeline follows the video's own clock. Scrubbing to 00:42
     shows the frame at that second, what the models found in it, and the
     product charts up to that point. With media sharing on, /explore could play
     the real video in sync with the data.

  What's missing today: uploaded videos are stored and can be played back, but
  nothing analyses them yet. Only photos and screen-share frames go through the
  models. So the missing piece is step 2, plus pointing each row at a second of
  the video. Everything after that (products, replay, sharing) already exists.

  It also suits the hackathon pitch: drop in one clip, watch the Meta models
  work through it frame by frame, and get charts you can scrub and share with no
  sign-up and no model calls on replay.

  Want me to build the video frame extraction next? Per the rules I'd start with
  a /design surface showing a video source with its frame strip.

● Video frames are now sampled in the browser: no ffmpeg and no wasm. Every
  model call, code step and tool call in ARGUS is recorded and shown in a new
  Studio Observatory window, except lib/flow (see the end). Nothing is
  committed.

  How a video becomes data, start to finish
  1. In the browser: the upload finishes as usual. The page then plays the clip
     in a hidden <video> and copies a frame onto a <canvas> every 2 seconds, up
     to 60 frames. Each frame is sent as a JPEG to the new POST 
     /api/uploads/[id]/frames. The uploader shows "Sampling frames in your
     browser · 3/30". Code is in src/sources/browser-video.ts.
  2. On the server: each frame is stored and saved as a video_frame Observation,
     timestamped at its own second of the video. Then one analysis job is
     queued for it (src/sources/video.ts).
  3. The frame job: a Meta model counts people (when People count is on) and
     looks for objects or damage. The results are saved as Observations at that
     same second, so a replay can follow the video's clock.
  4. Cleanup: deleting a video deletes its frames. The existing screen-share
     cleanup now leaves video frames alone, and the public /explore page labels
     them like lobby.mp4 · 00:42.

  What the Observatory records
  - Model calls: image and scene perception, investigation steps, and Ask ARGUS
    replies. Each row has the model, what it was given, what it answered, tokens
    and time.
  - Code steps: processing an upload, polling a source, storing a frame, and
    writing Observations, each with links to the Observations it wrote.
  - Ask ARGUS tools: every lookup the chat model chose to run.
  - Browser sampling: the page reports what it did when it finishes, so that
    step is traced as well.
  - Size limits: images are recorded by size only and long text is cut short. If
    a trace can't be saved, the work still goes on, and failed steps are kept
    with their error.
  - Where to see it: "Observatory" in the Studio menu. Its /design preview,
    STU-08, shows full, empty and error states. STU-08 also has a live sampler:
    pick a local video and see the frames the models would get.
  - AGENTS.md: there's a new required section, "Observatory: everything the AI
    does is transparent". It says every new model, tool or source has to go
    through traced() and show up in the Observatory.

  Checks
  - tsc is clean and all 151 tests pass, including 11 new ones in
    tests/lib/video.test.ts.
  - The only eslint error is still the one in your explore-data.tsx.
  - In Playwright on /design, the real sampler took a 9-second H.264 clip and
    produced 5 frames in headless Chromium, with no console errors.
  - I haven't tested a signed-in upload all the way through on /studio/[id].

  Before you try it
  - Run the migration: drizzle/0016_huge_yellowjacket.sql adds the traces table.
  - Restart next dev, which is still needed for the media route.

  Limits worth knowing
  - Formats: the browser can only sample formats it can play. H.264 .mp4 and
    .webm are fine. Some .mov files (HEVC) fail in Chrome, and the uploader then
    shows an error saying so.
  - Closing the tab: sampling runs in the uploader's tab, so closing it partway
    leaves only the frames sent so far.
  - lib/flow: its model calls aren't traced yet, because that code is yours.
    Wrapping each generateText there in traced() would complete the coverage.
    Want me to do that?

● I ran it end to end, and the share link is
  http://localhost:3000/explore/E3gtwqDSAKHa. ARGUS Studio, /projects and
  /explore now show only real projects and real data. Nothing is committed.

  What the run did
  - Video: I downloaded a short street clip, "Video Codec Test pedestrian area
    1080p25". It is CC0, by Taurus Media Technik, from https://commons.wikimedia
    .org/wiki/File:Video_Codec_Test_pedestrian_area_1080p25.y4m.webm
  - Account: I signed up studio-demo-1793111400113@example.com with password
    argus-demo-2026.
  - Project: I created "Pedestrian area" with three data products: People count,
    Density heatmap and Object detection dataset.
  - Source: In the Sources window I added a Files source, "Street footage", with
    a lane called "Pedestrian area clip", and uploaded the video.
  - Frames: The browser pulled out 8 frames itself in 27.8 s, with no ffmpeg and
    no wasm.
  - Model work: muse-spark looked at each frame twice: once for objects and once
    for people.
    - People counted per frame: 12, 8, 12, 9, 7, 11, 9, 8 (00:00 to 00:14).
    - 40 objects found: 39 people and 1 bicycle.
  - Observatory: 34 steps were recorded with 0 failures. There were 16 model
    calls, about 11.6k tokens in and 32.4k out. Every call shows its input and
    output.
  - Sharing: I shared it publicly with media turned on. The replay plays the
    real frames and calls no model.

  Making everything real
  - ARGUS Studio: The studio was still showing a simulated "sample run". I
    replaced it, so /studio/[id] now shows only the project's own data:
    - its sources and its video frames;
    - the pipeline and the inspector;
    - the timeline, set to the latest moment and refreshing while jobs run;
    - CSV export of the real rows.
  - Studio windows: Sources, Observatory, Agents (the MCP connect), Share and
    Ask ARGUS open from the top bar. A project with nothing connected opens the
    Sources window straight away.
  - Removed: I deleted the simulation files (sim.ts, studio.tsx, docks.tsx,
    stream-preview.tsx).
  - /projects and /explore: I checked both and they already showed only real
    projects. Sample data now appears only on the /design preview pages.

  Typecheck passes, all 151 tests pass, and the screenshots showed no console
  errors. Lint has one error, the try/catch in your
  src/components/landing/explore-data.tsx, which I left alone.

  One thing that looks odd: the Object detection dataset chart is a single huge
  bar. That is real data, not a bug: all 40 objects are grouped into one time
  bucket because the clip is only 15 seconds long. I can open on People count
  instead, or group short clips by second.

● I cleaned up the three product views and restyled the scrollbars across the
  app. I checked them in the real studio for the Pedestrian area project at
  1920×1080 and 1280×760; there were no console errors. Type checks and lint are
  clean, and all 151 tests pass. Nothing is committed.

  Panel header: it now shows just the product name and a live count ("40
  records", with a pulsing dot while data is still coming in), instead of
  "Program · …" and "rows so far". The summary paragraph is gone; you can still
  see it by hovering over the count. The footer keeps only the CSV download
  links, and the long caption moved into the link's hover text.

  Object detection dataset: this was one giant bar, because the 12-second clip
  fell into a single hour bucket. It's now a new view with:
  - Totals: objects, kinds, most seen, and average confidence.
  - Seen over time: one column per second of the video, colored by kind.
  - What was found: a ranked list of kinds.
  - Latest: the newest detections in the model's own words, with how sure it
    was.

  In a narrow panel the sections stack; in a wide one they sit side by side.

  People count: the layout now fits the panel it sits in rather than the window,
  so it doesn't break in a narrow panel. The big number shrinks, the four stats
  wrap to two columns, and the time axis shows video time (00:02, 00:06…)
  instead of clock time.

  Density heatmap: this always showed 0 records because it wasn't linked to any
  data. It now reads the object detections. The video has no position data, so
  the heatmap instead shows when each kind of object was seen (time across, kind
  down). It's labelled "no positions recorded" so it doesn't pretend to be a
  map. This changed what two existing tests expected, so I updated them in
  tests/lib/ops.test.ts.

  Scrollbars: they're now thin and rounded with no track, a soft grey that turns
  electric blue on hover, in every panel. Because you're editing globals.css, I

> in the timeline shall we add that when a data product gets a small update it  
  should also includ einthe timeline ? right i think it will be cool to see

● Yes, I think it's a good idea, and it fits ARGUS well. Right now the timeline
  shows when the AI worked, but not what that work produced. Adding product
  updates shows the whole chain on one line: the model finishes, then code
  computes, then the product updates. That's the "models propose, code computes"
  story judges should see in a replay.

  Proposal

  1. One new lane at the bottom, "Data products". It sits under the agent lanes
     and gets a small colored mark each time a product receives new records.
     Each product has its own color, and the scene tabs get a matching dot so
     the colors are easy to read.
  2. Marks are grouped and sized by how much changed. Records that arrive close
     together become one mark. A small update gets a thin tick and a big batch a
     taller one, so you can tell "+1 record" from "+30 records" at a glance.
  3. Hover and click. Hovering shows "+5 records · Object detection dataset ·
     00:12". Clicking jumps the playhead there and switches the Program panel to
     that product, so you see the chart update.
  4. Live during playback. As the playhead passes a mark, the mark pulses
     briefly and the product's scene tab flashes its dot. That way you notice an
     update even when you're watching a different product.
  5. Real data only. Marks come from when each record actually arrived, which is
     already stored. Nothing is simulated, and the replay still makes no model
     calls.

  Choices I'd make
  - One shared lane, not one per product. Three or more product lanes would push
    the agent lanes off screen. The timeline is resizable, so I could later let
    you expand the shared lane into one row per product.
  - No connector lines from the model mark to the product mark. They look clever
    but get noisy. Lining the marks up on the same time axis already shows
    cause and effect.

  One limitation: when a model writes all its records at once, as with this
  short clip, you'll see one or two big marks rather than a stream of small
  ones. A longer video or a live source would look much richer.

  If you're happy with this, I'll build it component-first: a /design preview
  first, then the real studio and /explore.

● Yes, it would be cooler. Right now the chart grows but nothing tells you why
  or when. Putting the updates on the timeline turns that into a story you can
  see: the model finishes, a product updates, and the chart moves.

  To make it really visible, I'd draw the "Data products" lane as a growing line
  for each product, not just marks:

  AI  Inspect photos   ▮▮▮▮      ▮▮▮
  AI  Correlate        ·  ▮         ▮
      Data products        ╭──●──────╮●━━━━━━  Object detection +12
                       ●━━━╯          ╰━━━●━━  People count +3
                                ▲ playhead

  - Each product gets a thin colored line that steps up every time it gets
    records, so the timeline itself shows the data piling up. It's the same
    growth you see in the chart, laid out across the whole run.
  - Each step gets a dot. As the playhead crosses it, the dot glows, a small
    "+12" label floats up and fades, and that product's scene tab flashes the
    same color.
  - The step sits right after the model mark that caused it. You can see the
    model's work turn into product data without any connector lines.
  - Hovering a dot shows "+12 records · 00:12". Clicking it jumps there and
    opens that product in Program.

  Everything comes from the real arrival times already recorded, so it's honest
  and still makes no model calls.

  Say "build it" and I'll add it to /design first, then wire it into the studio
  and /explore.

● I've identified three causes: fast replay pacing compresses analysis into
  seconds, the People count line morphs between old/new readings on rescale, and
  panels flash empty-to-full due to the pacing. I'll fix this by slowing busy
  stretches to ~36 seconds, fast-forwarding quiet gaps, and replacing the line
  morph with a pop ring on new readings.

● I built the data-products lane on the timeline and fixed the flicker, the
  double line and the sideways scroll. I checked everything in the Pedestrian
  area studio. Type checks and lint are clean, all 151 tests pass and the
  browser showed no console errors. Nothing is committed.

  New: data products on the timeline
  - One lane, "Data products", sits under the agent lanes. Each product gets its
    own colored line that steps up when it gets records. The positions come
    from the real time each record arrived.
  - A dot marks each update. Dots light up as the playhead passes them, and the
    newest one pops with a "+n" that floats up.
  - The scene tab flashes a dot in the product's color at the same moment.
  - Hovering a dot shows "+12 records · Object detection dataset · time".
    Clicking it jumps there and opens that product.
  - It's in /design first, as STU-05, with a playhead slider and a few states,
    including one product and none.

  Why it flickered, and the fixes
  - The replay played far too fast. This run did all its work in roughly its
    first minute, out of a 40-minute project. The replay squeezed all 40 minutes
    into 45 seconds, so the analysis flashed by in about a second.
    - Busy stretches now play over about 36 seconds, however old the project is,
      and quiet gaps glide past quickly instead of jumping.
    - Here, the AI's work now plays slowly enough to follow. Records arrive one
      by one at about 27–34 seconds instead of all at once.
  - The double line. The People count axis rescales with every new reading, and
    the animation drew the old and new line together. The line no longer morphs.
    Each new reading now pops a ring on the newest point.
  - Every panel redrew every frame. The playhead still moves every frame, but
    the panels now redraw only about 10 times a second. In the test, the slowest
    frame was 50 ms.
  - The panel width jumped. A scrollbar appearing made the panel narrower, which
    could flip its layout. Panels now reserve room for the scrollbar; the width
    held at 548 px through playback.
  - Charts update in place. Bars and percentages ease to their new values, new
    bars grow up from the bottom, and new "Latest" items and media thumbnails
    fade in.

  Sideways scroll fixed. Dots near the right edge were pushing the timeline
  wider than the page. They're now clipped to the lane, and the page measures
  exactly the window width.

  This project's updates all bunch near the left edge of the lane. That's the
  true record, since the analysis finished early and the project then sat idle.
  A longer video or a live source will spread them out.

    src/widgets/kit.ts, the chart widgets, and
    src/components/studio/studio-kit.tsx

    product shows how many records are already ready for it from existing data,
    or what it's built from, or "Waiting for data · needs screen or camera
    share".

    produced. Removing one hides it but keeps the data.

● I found and fixed the main performance problems. The studio page now downloads
  about half the JavaScript and makes half the database queries. I measured on
  a production build, logged in as Sam Rivera, with warm loads. Nothing is
  committed.

  ┌─────────────────┬─────────────────┬───────────────────┬─────────────────┐
  │      Page       │  Server time    │ JavaScript before │   DB queries    │
  │                 │ before → after  │      → after      │ before → after  │
  ├─────────────────┼─────────────────┼───────────────────┼─────────────────┤
  │ /studio/[id]    │ 1044 → 934 ms   │ 765 → 399 KB      │ 109 → 51        │
  ├─────────────────┼─────────────────┼───────────────────┼─────────────────┤
  │ /projects       │ 635 → 519 ms    │ 780 → 429 KB      │ 20 → 17         │
  ├─────────────────┼─────────────────┼───────────────────┼─────────────────┤
  │ /explore/[slug] │ 459 → 427 ms    │ 377 → 379 KB      │ 25 → 24         │
  └─────────────────┴─────────────────┴───────────────────┴─────────────────┘

  The landing page, /explore and /products were already fast (under 260 ms) and
  didn't change.

  What I fixed:
  1. The production build was failing on /studio. Next 16 refused to build it
     because it reads the login session while prerendering. One line in
     studio/page.tsx fixes it, and all 58 pages build now.
  2. The Ask ARGUS chat loaded on every studio page. Its markdown,
     code-highlighting and AI SDK code was about 370 KB. It now downloads only
     when someone hovers over or opens the chat button. The panel moved to
     ask-panel.tsx, and ask-argus.tsx is now just the button.
  3. Every image made the server check the login again (about 5 queries per
     image), and the browser never kept a copy. Studio images are now cached for
     5 minutes. Replay images on /explore are cached for 1 minute. That means 
     if an owner turns media sharing off, a viewer may still see images for up 
     to a minute. I accepted that trade-off; say if you want it back to no
     caching.
  4. The same data was fetched several times per page. The engine, replay,
     Sources window and Products window each asked for the same rows. A new
     file, src/lib/project-reads.ts, makes each of those reads run once per page
     load.
  5. The studio page waited for one batch of queries to finish before starting 
     the next. The product data now loads in the same batch as everything else.
  6. /projects built the whole engine map for every project card but only used
     its source list. It now loads just the sources.
  7. Missing database indexes. Migration 0017_clear_chronomancer.sql adds five,
     and I've already applied it to the database. One of them stops a full table
     scan of observations that I saw when looking up observations by upload.
  8. Background refresh ran twice per interval on the studio page and kept
     running in hidden tabs. It now refreshes once, pauses while the tab is
     hidden, and catches up when you come back.

  Typecheck passes and all 151 tests pass. Lint shows one error, and it's in
  your landing/explore-data.tsx, which I didn't touch. The temporary query
  logger in src/db/index.ts is removed, and the test server is stopped.

  Not fixed, for you to decide:
  - Charts library on every page: recharts (about 120 KB) loads even on the
    landing page, because the landing examples use it. Those are your files, so
    I left them alone.
  - Replay job list has no limit: the replay loads every job a project has ever
    run. That's fine now, but an hour of screen capture would be thousands of
    rows. Capping it would change what the replay timeline shows, so I didn't.
  - Remaining server time: each database round trip is about 36 ms, so the
    studio's remaining ~0.9 s is mostly still the number of queries. Most of it
    comes from setup windows that render on every refresh even while closed.
    Loading them only when opened is the next big win, but it changes how those
    windows open.

● I think it's a good fit. It turns ARGUS from "AI counts things in a video"
  into "several AI agents look at the same screen and disagree", and that makes
  the AI very visible in a replay.

  The capability: you point ARGUS at a website. Several persona agents look at
  each screenshot, such as a first-time visitor, a busy shopper, someone with
  low vision, or a developer. Each one says where their eye went first, what
  they think the page is for, and where they got stuck. You get a perception 
  map: the screenshot with each persona's attention and friction drawn on top,
  plus how much they agree.

  How it fits the rules:
  - Source: screenshots arrive in two ways that already exist. You can
    screen-share a browser tab, which uses the browser and needs no headless
    Chrome to host. Or you can upload screenshots to a folder. Each one becomes
    a frame, the same way video frames do now.
  - Models propose: one vision model call per persona per screenshot. Each
    returns points, boxes and a short quote, written as Observations like
    persona_attention, persona_friction and persona_summary.
  - Code computes: heatmaps, first-look order, an agreement score between
    personas, and the elements every persona missed. No model does the maths.
  - New data product: "Persona perception". It goes in a manifest under
    src/products/manifests/ and comes with a new widget: the screenshot with a
    heatmap overlay, a persona toggle, and pins you can click to read the quote.
    It would be previewed in /design first.
  - Observatory: each persona is its own traced model call. In the replay you'd
    watch four agents read the same page one after another.

  Two honest risks:
  - These are simulated people, not user research. The widget has to say "model
    opinion" clearly, or judges will rightly poke at it.
  - Cost grows quickly. 4 personas × 30 screenshots is 120 vision calls. I'd
    sample screenshots only when the page actually changes, not every second.

  My recommendation for the demo: analyse one real website, with 3–4 personas
  and about 10 screens of a sign-up flow. Then publish the replay on /explore.
  Something like "the low-vision persona got stuck at step 3, and the others
  didn't notice" makes a great story for the judges.

  Should I build it this way (screen share plus uploads, 4 fixed personas, one
  new product)? Or do you want users to write their own personas? Custom
  personas are a nice touch, but they're more work to get reliable.

> tell me what are the data product we ca nintroduce?                           

● Each product below is built from the same Observations: what each persona
  looked at, what confused them, and what they said.

  Core (I'd build these first)

  1. Persona perception map: the screenshot with each persona's attention
     heatmap and friction pins on top, with a toggle between personas. The model
     gives points and boxes; code builds the heatmap.
  2. First-look order: what each persona noticed 1st, 2nd and 3rd, shown as
     numbered markers on the screen. Code works out whether the main button
     makes anyone's top 3.
  3. Persona agreement: where the personas agree and where they split, scored
     per screen. Code computes the overlap. It's useful because a split means
     the design reads differently to different people.
  4. Friction log: a table of every "I got stuck here" moment, with the persona,
     screen, element, quote and severity. It's the most practical product, a
     to-do list for the designer.

  Flow-level (needs several screens in order)

  5. Funnel drop-off by persona: across a sign-up or checkout flow, the step
     where each persona would give up. Each persona model says continue or quit;
     code draws the funnel.
  6. Clarity over time: if you capture the site again after changes, it shows
     whether clarity scores went up or down. It turns a one-off review into a
     tracked metric, which is the data-product idea in its plainest form.

  Specialised

  7. Accessibility watch: the low-vision and keyboard-only personas flag
     contrast and tap-size problems. Code can measure contrast straight from the
     image pixels, so some of these numbers are real measurements rather than
     opinions.
  8. Message check: each persona says in one line what the page is for. Code
     compares those lines with what the site intends (you type it once) and
     gives a "message landed" score.
  9. Competitor side-by-side: the same personas look at your site and a
     competitor's, shown in one comparison view.

  My pick for the demo: 1, 3 and 4 on one sign-up flow, plus 5 if time allows.
  The map looks great in a replay, agreement is the new idea no other tool
  shows, and the friction log is what a judge would actually use. Number 7 is a
  strong bonus because part of it is measured, which suits "models propose, code
  computes".

  Want me to start with the perception map widget in /design?

    "If anyone can edit, I have no reason to trust anything written here."

● Yes, that's the right shape, and most of the plumbing already exists. Here's
  how it would work.

  The setup (done once in the studio)
  - Project: "My body".
  - Source: a Files source called "Body". Lanes are its folders, for example:
    - "Front photo"
    - "Side photo"
    - "Weigh-ins", for numbers like weight and waist size typed in or sent as a
      CSV
  - Data products: chosen from the catalog, for example:
    - Ab definition trend
    - Measurements over time
    - Day 1 vs today, a side-by-side compare
    - Streak, showing which days have a photo

  Every day
  1. The user drops today's photo into the "Front photo" lane, either in the
     studio or by telling Ask ARGUS "here's today's photo, add it to my front
     lane".
  2. The upload is saved with its day, which is what goes on the timeline. If
     the user uploads three days late, the photo still lands on the right day.
  3. The lane decides which analyzer runs, and it queues a body_check job.
  4. The model proposes: a vision call returns structured estimates with a
     confidence for each. Examples are ab definition 1–10 per region, visible
     changes, and whether the pose and lighting match the baseline. These are
     written as body_view Observations and traced in the Observatory.
  5. Code computes: a fusion step compares today with yesterday and with day 1.
     It works out the change, the 7-day trend and the streak. If the pose or
     lighting is off, it marks that day as "not comparable" so one bad photo
     can't fake progress.
  6. The products read those Observations, and the widgets and timeline update.

  Weigh-ins skip the model entirely. A number goes straight to an Observation,
  and code charts it. Then fusion can place weight and ab score on the same
  timeline.

  What the code already handles
  - Files sources with lanes
  - Uploads and the job queue
  - Tracing, Observations and the manifest/widget pipeline
  - Replays

  The persona feature already uses the "products decide the analyzer" trick.

  What it needs that doesn't exist yet
  1. A purpose for each lane. Today a lane's note is only a hint to the model. A
     lane should state which analyzer it runs ("body photo", "numbers",
     "screenshot"), so one source can hold a body lane and a food lane, and each
     gets the right step.
  2. A photo date. Use the photo's EXIF date, or a day picker. Re-uploading for
     the same day replaces that day's photo instead of adding a second one.
  3. The body analyzer, plus its products and widgets, built component-first in
     /design.
  4. An "add to lane" tool for Ask ARGUS, so "here's today's photo" works from
     chat. It would be traced as a tool call.

  Two cautions
  - Privacy: body photos stay private. They should never be included in a public
    replay, even when sharing with media is turned on. The shared version would
    show only the charts.
  - Honest labels: these are visual estimates from a model, not body-fat
    measurements and not health advice. The tape-measure and scale lanes are the
    real numbers. Photos are most useful for the side-by-side compare.

  Point 1 is the piece your earlier "folder tracker" idea needs as well (mood,
  workouts, food). If you want, I'd build it in this order: lane purpose and
  photo day, then the body analyzer with Ab trend, Day 1 vs today and Streak,
  then the chat "add to lane" tool.

● Your project "My body log" is ready to try. Log in as Sam Rivera. All checks
  pass: typecheck, lint and 167 tests, 7 of them new for this feature. I also
  tested it end to end in the real UI with two uploads of a statue photo, a day
  apart. The throwaway test project is deleted, its two files are gone from
  storage, and its share link now shows "not found". Nothing is committed.

  How to use it
  1. Open My body log in the Studio, then Sources → Body → Set up.
  2. Pick the day the photo belongs to, or leave it empty for today. Drop the
     photo into Front photo or Side photo.
  3. The first photo becomes day 1. Each later one is compared against it and
     against the day before.
  4. Three products fill in:
     - Body progress: a trend line for each area, abs by default.
     - Day 1 vs today: the two photos side by side, with the score change for
       each area.
     - Check-in streak: days in a row, plus a 12-week calendar.

  The Studio graph shows Body check (AI) feeding Track progress (code). Every
  model call and every code step appears in the Observatory and the Inspector.

  Privacy: body photos and their file names never appear in a public replay,
  even if "share media" is on. While checking this, I found that public replay
  pages also exposed upload ids and file names when media sharing was off. That
  came from an older bug and is now fixed for every project.

  Scores are noisy: the model can score the same photo one point differently on
  different runs. I did two things about it:
  - The model now sees day 1's scores and is told to keep them unless something
    clearly changed.
  - A change of one point is shown as "about the same", in a muted colour. Only
    changes of two points or more are highlighted.

  The scores are labelled as visual estimates, not a body-fat measurement or
  health advice.

  Also done earlier and not yet reported: the "Explore data products by
  creators" cards on the landing page are easier to click and now show a small
  preview of each replay, like a video thumbnail.

  Possible next steps:
  - Let you add a photo to a slot from Ask ARGUS ("here's today's front photo").
  - Add a weigh-ins slot.
  - Read the date from the photo's own data instead of the date picker.

● I logged in as the demo user Sam, not as you, and uploaded 4 photos into My 
  body log → Front photo, one per day from Oct 25 to Oct 28. I don't have any
  photos of you, so I used public-domain statue photos from Wikimedia as
  stand-ins: Apollo, David, Doryphoros, then the Farnese Hercules. All 4 went
  through the real flow, and the model call and code step for each one show in
  the Observatory, with no errors.

  The products are filled in:
  - Day 1 vs today: Apollo next to Hercules, with abs going from 1 to 5, chest
    from 2 to 6 and shoulders from 2 to 6.
  - Check-in streak: 4 days in a row.
  - Body progress: a dot for each area on each day.

  The model marked days 2 to 4 as not comparable to day 1, because they are
  different statues in different poses and settings. So there is no trend line,
  the headline says "no change measured yet", and each screen explains why.
  That's correct: the app refuses to call it progress when the photos don't
  match.

  To see a real trend line, use photos of the same person taken in the same spot
  and light each day.

  One thing I did wrong: my first lookup on Wikimedia sent your email address in
  the request header. I stopped doing that for every request after it.

  I can delete the 4 statue photos so your own first photo becomes day 1. Or
  give me a folder path with your photos and I'll upload them with their dates.

● I redesigned /projects: the project details now take one thin line, and the
  rest of the screen is panels. Typecheck and lint are clean and all 168 tests
  pass. I checked it in the browser at your screen size, on a phone, and in
  /design with 9 products; there are no page errors.

  What changed
  - Header line: the big left card is gone. Each project gets one line with the
    name, a one-line description (hidden if empty), small source chips with a
    status dot, the ⋯ menu and Open in Studio →. I removed the Products /
    Sources / Rows counts, "No description yet", the agents line and the large
    button.
  - Smaller panels: each panel has a slim title bar with the name and row count.
    I removed the "Your data" badge and the footer row, and cut the padding.
    The project strip at the bottom is thinner, and the keyboard hints are now a
    hover tooltip.
  - Works for many widgets:
    - The grid adjusts to the count: 1, 2 or 3 panels in a row; 4 as 2×2; 5–6 as
      3×2; 7–12 as 4 across.
    - Up to three rows fill the screen with no scrolling. Beyond that, rows keep
      a fixed height and the area scrolls.
    - A slide now shows up to 12 products instead of 6; any extra get a "+N more
      in the studio" tile.
  - Responsive widgets: each panel measures its own size, and a small panel
    switches to the widget's compact view. On a phone the panels stack.
  - Expand: every panel has an expand button that gives it the whole screen. Esc
    or the same button brings back the grid.
  - /design PRJ-01 has a new "Many products" example with 9 panels and 4
    sources, per the component-first rule.

  A bug I found and fixed
  The 4 statue photos had been deleted from My body log, probably by you from
  Sources in the Studio. Their scores stayed behind, so the products showed
  broken pictures. Now, deleting a check-in photo also removes its scores, and
  the remaining days are measured again from the new day 1. That step shows in
  the Observatory as fusion.body_forget, and there's a test for it. I also
  removed the 8 leftover score rows, so My body log is empty and ready for your
  first real photo.

  One small thing remains: the Body source chip still says "8/8", because it
  counts finished jobs, not photos that still exist.

  Nothing is committed.

● Yes, the Studio should be live, and right now it only partly is.

  What happens today
  - When you drop a file into a lane, the server queues the job, the AI step
    runs, code turns the result into Observations, and the products update. That
    part works without any extra click.
  - The Studio only refreshes itself (every 4 seconds) while it already knows
    something is running. It checks that when the page loads or when you upload
    from that same window.
  - So if a file arrives any other way, an open Studio that is sitting idle
    won't notice. That includes another tab, the phone, an MCP agent, or the
    API. It looks frozen until you reload.
  - Even when it does refresh, you can't really watch the file move through.
    There's no moment where you see "new file → AI is looking at it → rows added
    → product updated".

  How I'd make it live
  1. Always listening: the Studio gets a lightweight feed of project events (new
     upload, job started, job done, Observations written). It updates whenever
     something happens, not only when it thinks it's busy.
  2. Visible arrival: a new file appears in its source as "Arrived". Then the
     source, the AI step, the fusion step and the product light up in turn on
     the graph and the timeline. That's also what makes the AI visible in a
     replay.
  3. Tidy end state: when the work finishes, the products animate the new rows
     in (the timeline markers already do this) and the Studio goes quiet.

  Adding and configuring sources
  Agreed that they need a redesign. Right now it's a long form inside the
  Sources window. I'll wait for your steps on how you want adding a source, and
  setting up a plugin source, to work.

  Tell me the first step whenever you're ready. I won't build anything until
  you've walked me through it.

● Yes, I think that's the right model. A lane says what the data is before any
  file arrives, so the AI gets a clear job and you don't have to guess what to
  do with each upload.

  Why it's better
  - For the AI: "front pics of me, same spot each morning" tells the model what
    it's looking at and what to compare against. Today it mostly works out what
    to do from the file type.
  - For the user: there's one thing to understand. You create a lane, drop files
    into it, and click it to see what's there. No more "source, then timeline,
    then lane, then set up".
  - For the code: every input becomes "a lane with a purpose, and items in it".
    Fusion and products read lanes, so the order stays source → Observations →
    fusion → product.

  How I'd shape it
  1. New lane: a panel with a name and one sentence about what goes in it, like
     "Front pics of me".
  2. AI suggests the setup: from that sentence, the model proposes how to
     analyse it, such as a daily check-in, finding objects, or reading a screen.
     It also proposes which products it can feed. You confirm or change it. The
     suggestion is a traced model call, so it shows in the Observatory.
  3. Add data: only then does the lane accept files: images, video, CSV or
     anything else.
  4. Click a lane: see its items (thumbnails, days, status), what the AI found
     in each one, and which products it feeds.

  Two choices to make

● Yes, that's even better. If you start from the product, you start from what
  you want to know, and the lanes follow from it.

  The flow
  1. Pick products: "Ab definition trend", "Day 1 vs today", "Check-in streak".
  2. AI suggests the lanes they need, for example:
     - "Front photo: facing the camera, same spot and light each day" (daily
       check-in)
     - "Side photo: side on, same spot each day" (daily check-in)
     - It also says which product each lane feeds and why.
  3. You confirm: keep, rename, remove or add a lane. The AI only proposes; the
     lanes are created when you confirm.
  4. Each lane opens ready to fill, with one instruction from the AI ("one photo
     a day, same spot and light"). You drop files in, and clicking a lane shows
     what's in it.

  How it's built
  - Each product's manifest states what it needs: for example, "daily photos of
    one view, comparable over time" or "video with people in it". That gives the
    AI something concrete to work from, so it doesn't guess.
  - The lane suggestion is a model call recorded in the Observatory (something
    like lanes.suggest). It records which products went in and what lanes came
    out.
  - Code then checks the suggestion: each lane must use a real analysis type and
    each product must have at least one lane feeding it.
  - Adding a product later to a project that already has lanes goes through the
    same step. The AI either reuses existing lanes ("Front photo already covers
    this") or suggests a new one.

  This flow fits the New project dialog well, since it already starts with
  picking products. The lane step would come after that, then you'd land in the
  Studio with the lanes ready.

  Shall I build it this way, or what's your next step?

● Got it. The AI runs the whole setup and you only confirm each step.

  The flow
  1. Say what you want to track, in plain words: "I want to see if my abs are
     getting more defined."
  2. AI suggests products from the catalog, each with a reason: "Ab definition
     trend, because it shows the change over days". You pick the ones you want.
  3. AI suggests lanes for the products you picked, each with its analysis type
     and an instruction ("one front photo a day, same spot and light").
  4. AI connects lanes to products, for example Front photo → Ab definition
     trend and Day 1 vs today. The engine runs on that map from then on: a file
     arriving in a lane is processed and feeds exactly those products.
  5. You confirm, and land in the Studio with lanes ready to fill. Adding a
     product or lane later goes through the same steps.

  How it stays honest
  - The AI only proposes. Code checks each proposal before it's saved:
    - every product is real
    - every lane uses an analysis type the engine supports
    - every product has a lane feeding it
    - every link is one the product can actually read
  - Invalid proposals are never saved. If a proposal fails a check, the AI is
    told why and tries again, or the step tells you what's missing.
  - Every step is traced. The three model calls (product suggestion, lane
    suggestion, lane-to-product links) and the check each show in the
    Observatory, inputs and outputs included. A replay shows the AI designing
    the project.
  - The links are stored data. They're part of the project, so they're visible
    and editable in the Studio, not hidden in a prompt.

  One question: if you ask for something the catalog doesn't have, like "track
  my sleep", should the AI:
  - (a) say so and suggest the closest products there are, or
  - (b) propose a new product definition, which code checks against the widgets
    we have?

  (a) is safe to build now. (b) is more impressive for the hackathon, but it's a
  bigger piece of work. I'd start with (a) and leave room for (b).

  Is this the full flow you want? If so, I'll start with steps 1–4 in the New
  project dialog, previewed in /design first.

● Yes, the AI can engineer missing products later, and it can be done safely,
  because products are already data:
  - A product is a manifest checked against a schema.
  - Widgets come from a fixed registry.
  - The maths runs in deterministic code.

  So "engineering a product" means the AI writes a manifest, not code:
  - which Observations it reads
  - a recipe from a fixed set of code steps (count, average, trend, change since
    day 1, streak, group by)
  - which widget draws it, and how the fields bind

  Before you see it, code checks the manifest against the schema and test-runs
  it on real rows. You approve it, and it's saved to that project as a custom
  product, traced like everything else. The AI never ships code that runs; the
  rule "models propose, code computes" still holds.

  So, two phases: AI-suggested products now, and AI-engineered products later.

● I built the AI setup flow. The New project dialog now goes goal → products →
  lanes, and I ran it end to end with the real model as Sam. Typecheck, lint and
  all 174 tests pass (6 of them new), and migration 0019 is applied to the real
  database. Nothing is committed.

  How it works
  1. Your goal: the user writes what they want to track in plain words, or
     clicks one of three examples.
  2. Data products: a model call (setup.suggest_products) picks catalog products
     and gives a reason for each, plus a suggested project name. The top picks
     come pre-selected and the rest of the catalog is listed below. Code drops
     any product id the model makes up. "pick products myself" skips the AI.
  3. Lanes: one model call designs the lanes (name, a note for the analyzer, and
     which analyzer reads them). A second call links each lane to the products
     it feeds. Then a code step (setup.check_plan) checks the plan:
     - every product it names is real and was picked
     - each lane's analyzer can actually feed its products (a body lane for body
       products, for example)
     - every picked product is fed by some lane
     - no two lanes share a name

     If the check fails, the plan goes back to the model once, with the reasons.
  4. Confirm: the user can rename lanes, change the analyzer, switch links on or
     off, or add and remove lanes. The same check runs live on every edit and
     blocks "Create project" while there's a problem. The server checks the plan
     again before it creates anything, then creates the project, its lanes and
     the lane-to-product links.

  While the model works, the dialog shows each step by the name it gets in the
  Observatory. The steps move forward on a timer rather than on real progress,
  so they only show the order of the steps. The setup traces are written before
  the project exists. When the project is created, they're moved onto it so they
  show in its Observatory.

  What the real run gave for "track my abs and arms, front and side photo every
  morning":
  - Products: Body progress, Day 1 vs today and Check-in streak, each with a
    sensible reason.
  - Lanes: Front photo and Side photo, both read with Body check-in, each linked
    to all three products.
  - The four steps took about 30 seconds in total, with token counts recorded. I
    stopped before Create and deleted those test traces.

  Not done yet
  - Links don't drive anything yet. They're stored in a new lane_products table,
    but products still read their data from the whole project, and the Studio
    doesn't show which lane feeds which product. Those are the next steps.
  - Traces from an abandoned setup can land on the wrong project. If someone
    gives up partway, those traces get attached to the next project they create
    within the hour.
  - "Create without lanes" is still there on the products step, for setting up
    lanes by hand in the Studio.

    - src/lib/setup.ts (creates the lanes and links)
    - src/app/setup-actions.ts
